title: Manna (Exodus 16)
hook: bread from heaven, enough for each day, and a double portion before Shabbat

segments.voice: Yesterday, Miriam's timbrel, the drum the women packed before there was anything to celebrate. Your line was bring the drum. Now the food runs out.

Open a fridge and look at it the way a desert traveler would. Leftovers in the back you forgot about. Three kinds of mustard. A lot of us stock up, just in case, because tomorrow feels uncertain. A month out of Egypt, the Israelites are in the wilderness, and the food from Egypt has run out. They complain: back in Egypt we sat by pots of meat and ate our fill. And God answers with a strange promise: bread will fall from the sky every morning. But you can only take enough for today.
screen: `THE FOOD RUNS OUT.` → `BACK IN EGYPT WE ATE OUR FILL.` → `BREAD FROM THE SKY, ONE DAY AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: God says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Behold, I will cause to rain bread from heaven for you." Next morning the dew lifts, and on the ground there's something fine and flaky, like frost. The people say to each other, man hu? What is it? "For they knew not what it was." The name sticks: man, manna, is basically the word what. They ate a question for forty years. The Torah says it was white, like coriander seed, and tasted like wafers made with honey. The rabbis added that it tasted like whatever each person wanted. Now the rules. Each person gathers about an omer, a measure of a day's food. Some gather more, some less, and when they measure it, nobody has too much and nobody too little. Don't keep any until morning. Some people do anyway, and by morning it's full of worms and stinks. Except for one day. On the sixth day, everyone finds twice as much, and the extra keeps overnight, because on the seventh day nothing falls. So in the wilderness the people keep a Shabbat, and it comes with a double portion. Tradition links that to the two loaves on the Shabbat table today; more on them later. The rabbis saw manna as a daily school of trust. You couldn't hoard it. You had to go out each morning and find there was enough, again. Moses later puts it this way: people don't live by bread alone. And a jar of manna, the story says, was kept for future generations to see.
screen: `MAN HU? WHAT IS IT?` · `EVERYONE HAD ENOUGH.` · `NONE LEFT OVER, EXCEPT FOR SHABBAT.` · `A DAILY SCHOOL OF TRUST.` · then, large: `I WILL CAUSE TO RAIN BREAD FROM HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you tend to over-gather: food, clothes, tabs open on your phone, worry about next week. Hold it up to the manna rule, enough for today and no more, and ask what enough looks like, just for today. Then set the rest down for now, like a bag you've been carrying for no reason.
Manna. From man hu, what is it? Bread from heaven, gathered each morning, enough for one day, and double before Shabbat.
Your line: enough for today. Each morning in the wilderness, there was enough again. Ninety-two days in.

howItsDone: Jews recall the manna every Shabbat with two loaves of challah on the table, and some say a reading about the manna in daily prayers as a lesson in trust.

fork.setup: you've gathered your manna, and there's a little left over tonight. you're worried about tomorrow. what do you do?
options: keep it for the morning, just in case.
eat what you need and leave none.
fork.reveal: the rule was leave none until morning. those who kept it found worms. only the sixth day's double portion kept, for Shabbat.

original.note: Hebrew: manna. the people's question, man hu, what is it, became its name.

trapdoor: what it means: food for one day at a time, with a double portion for Shabbat, a daily lesson in trust.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 16:15 plays on man hu, what is it; the rabbis said it tasted like whatever each person wished (Yoma 75a).

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Exodus 16:4 and 16:15.
'A month after the sea' is an approximation from Exodus 16:1 (the fifteenth day of the second month). Confirm.
'The first Shabbat the people keep in the Torah' — Exodus 16:23–30 is commonly described this way. Confirm.
Daily recitation of the manna passage (Parashat HaMan) is a custom in some communities. Confirm framing in howItsDone.
Manna tasted as each wished: Yoma 75a; confirm.

Editor review: 'a month after the sea' corrected to 'a month out of Egypt' (16:1 counts from the departure); cut the superlative 'the first Shabbat'; the two-loaves custom is now 'tradition links', not 'that's why'.
